Out of Turn

Burst Monitor · the read from the Friday, November 20 close

Out of Turn

The S&P 500 lost 8.6% last week, its worst week since April 2025, and closed lower for a seventh straight session. For five months this market's largest moves have set one group against another, the AI stocks falling as most others rose or the reverse, so that each side's losses were partly cushioned by the other's gains. Last week the cushion thinned. On Monday one side fell hardest, on Tuesday the other, on Thursday almost everything fell at once, and on Friday the first side fell again, far harder. An instrument built to watch how the five hundred move together shows the two groups still standing well apart while more of their movement became shared. Here is what it saw, in plain terms, with two figures you can play, how firm each part is, and what repair would look like.

If you are new here · the story so far, in four lines

Since July
When the S&P 500 moves, its stocks usually move together: an up day lifts nearly all of them. Since July the biggest shared move has instead been two-sided, one group rising while another falls. The record back to 2000 has nothing like it for longer than a few weeks. This is month five.
October
The index made a record on October 6, carried by its largest names. Over the next weeks the rally rotated away from them: the AI complex (Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, Meta, Alphabet and the names that trade with them) fell while most other stocks rose. On October 21 the instrument fixed the two groups by name, 314 stocks in the rally group and 114 in the AI group, so nothing could be re-sorted after the fact.
Last week
The index rebounded 2.5%. The previous edition, Closing Ranks, found it was mostly one group's rebound, with each group moving more tightly than at any point this autumn. It named the reading that would mean real trouble: the two groups starting to fall together.
This week
That reading arrived in part. The two groups are as far apart as they have been, and they have moved the same way on many days before. What changed is the degree: two of this week's declines were the most widely shared in six months, and the offset between the groups protected the typical stock less than it had.

The read in one paragraph. The board shows two groups remaining far apart while more of their movement becomes shared. Several of this week's declines reached both groups, though the hard-hit names fell about three times as far. By Friday, stocks from both sides were concentrated at a recent low in their own swing or still descending toward one, with very few rising. The separation persisted; the offset between the groups, which had cushioned the typical stock for months, offered less protection. That combination is compatible with broader pressure reaching both sides, though the board does not identify a source. It also leaves room for a rebound, and a gathering near recent lows does not establish that the decline is finished. The analyst's lean remains down, held less firmly than a week ago, with the next sessions to be judged against the repair markers in chapter 5.

1 · The week

One side, then the other, then everyone, then the first side again

The index fell on all five sessions, and each of the four real declines had a different cast. That sequence is the story of the week, more than its total.

Two words first. The S&P 500 is cap-weighted: each company counts in proportion to its market value, so its ten largest listings, well over a third of the value, can pull the index away from what most of its members did. The typical stock here is the median: the one in the middle when all five hundred are lined up by their returns.

The week, day by day

each session's return: the index, the typical stock of all 500, the AI group and the rally group · the label over each day is the share of the 500 that rose

Monday was the AI group's day. Its typical member lost 2.7% while the rally group's lost a third of one percent. Tuesday reversed the roles: the rally group fell 1.4% and the AI group 1.0%, and the typical stock lost more than the index did. Wednesday was a pause. Nvidia had reported results the evening before that were stronger than expected, and the market did little with them.

Thursday was the broad one. The index opened more than a percent higher and closed 2.0% lower, and only 7 of every 100 stocks rose. Both groups fell by nearly the same amount. Friday was the largest index decline of the four, 3.7%, and a lopsided one underneath: the AI group's typical member lost 4.4%, the rally group's lost 0.6%, a quarter of all stocks rose, and consumer staples finished higher. Friday looked like the worst day of the week because the largest companies were the ones falling. For the typical stock Thursday was worse.

group (held fixed by name since Oct 21)namesMonTueThuFrithe weekhigher on the weeksince Oct 6

Each row is the median of its members' own returns, not a portfolio. The two groups are the instrument's October 21 selections, not industry categories, and they do not cover the whole index. The ten are the ten largest listings shown: nine companies, with Alphabet trading as two lines.

A simple measure makes the sequence visible across a longer stretch. For each session, put every stock's move in units of that stock's own usual daily swing, then ask how much of the day's total movement is a single shift shared by all of them. Call it the day's common share. On an ordinary day it is small, about 7%, because stocks mostly go their own ways.

How much of each day was one shared move

the common share of every session since late May, 126 in all · gold = this week · the dotted line is the six-month median

Thursday's common share was 60%, the highest of the 126 sessions. Tuesday's was 51%, the second highest. Friday's, even with the AI group falling seven times as far as the rally group, was 37%, the sixth. Five of the top six fall inside the last twelve sessions; one of the five is the rebound of November 9, a shared move upward. More of this market's movement has been shared in November than at any time since May, in both directions.

The same shows up between the two groups directly. They have often moved the same way on a given day, last week's rebound included. What is new is how closely. Over the last 21 sessions the daily moves of the rally group and the AI group ran together with a correlation of +0.53. In each of the five earlier 21-session stretches back to May it was between −0.50 and +0.28. The offset between them has weakened; it has not vanished, as Monday and Friday show.

The instrument's slower gauge of the same thing is the story count: the effective number of independent patterns in the stocks' daily returns. Twenty would mean twenty separate stories. A count collapsing toward three or four means one move has taken over, which is what the market looked like on the way into 2008, March 2020 and the spring of 2025.

The story count since August

21-session reader (ink) and 63-session reader (gold), by morning · each morning's reading uses returns through the session before, so the hollow markers are the windows that end on Friday itself

The slow reader stood at 19.5 in mid-October. It is now 11.0, its lowest since August 2025, and 10.8 once Friday's returns are included. The fast reader has stopped falling: it has sat between 5.8 and 6.1 since November 13. It has not turned up. And the count is still falling into two stories, not one. The biggest shared pattern carries 34% of the market's day-to-day variation, close to its long-run middle, while the second pattern, the one that separates the two groups, carries 20%, more than twice its usual share and up again with Friday included.

What the week cost is easiest to see against the record. Since October 6 the index is down 11.6%. A week ago its typical stock was still 7.3% above where it stood that day. Now it is 1.4% above, and 54 of every 100 members are higher. The rally group is up 6.1% from the record. The AI group is down 17.3%.

The two groups did not merge. More of what they did, they did together.

Outside the instrument · the analyst's layer, kept separate

The instrument reads prices only, by design. Its job is to say where the pressure and the coordination are, not why. Everything in this box is the analyst's: dated facts, an explanation they are compatible with, views stated before their outcomes, and what would weaken each.

The facts, dated against the sessions. Tuesday Nov 17, after the close: Nvidia reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion against about $109 billion expected and guided to $130 billion for the next quarter, its first report since its chief executive resigned. The stock rose in late trading and fell 2.9% on Wednesday. Thursday Nov 19: Anthropic began trading after pricing its shares at $83; they opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17. The S&P 500 opened more than a percent higher and closed 2.0% lower. Friday Nov 20, 2:13 pm ET: Reuters reported, citing sources, that a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation of Nvidia is examining potential accounting issues. Nvidia was already down more than 6% before the report and closed down 14.0%; an inquiry is not a finding. The Philadelphia semiconductor index lost 10.7%, the Nasdaq Composite 5.3%, and a widely used measure of expected volatility closed at 35.9. Over the week the two-year Treasury yield fell from 4.88% to 4.63% and the ten-year from 5.15% to 4.92%. U.S. markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday. The Federal Reserve meets December 8–9.

A compatible explanation. A confidence shock specific to AI hardware is running inside a broader withdrawal from stocks. The first accounts for Friday's extreme losses in chips and for staples holding up. The second is needed for Tuesday and Thursday, when the names that had been sheltering investors fell too, and for a week in which 94 of every 100 stocks finished lower. A further rise in Treasury yields was not this week's explanation, since yields fell through the week. Falling yields alongside falling stocks are consistent with investors moving toward safety; they do not show it.

The analyst's views, stated before their outcomes. November 10: no ordinary post-midterm bounce, with the rally group rolling over and the two crowds converging. Since that day's close the index has lost 8.1%; the rally group did roll over and the down days did become shared ones; on the map the two crowds have not converged, they have moved further apart. Wednesday November 18, before the open: the direction is down, a bounce will not hold, and the index will close below Tuesday's 7,340.53 by December 2. It did so that afternoon. Friday November 20, before the open: the rising quarter of the dial will not fill today. It held 8 names of 500.

The view for the week ahead, stated Sunday November 22. Still down, held less firmly than a week ago: Monday flat to lower, and the shortened week lower overall, with the index closing below 6,910.39 on Monday and on Friday the 27th. The analyst is watching each session for the board to show a break in the present pattern, expects one eventually and does not claim to know when; some of the hardest-hit names are placed to swing up. The calendar leans the other way: on this instrument's own index series the S&P 500 has finished Thanksgiving week higher in 19 of the last 26 years, and in four of the six that began at least 8% below a high.

What would weaken each. Against the hardware-shock reading: the split between the two groups began in July, long before any of this week's news, and the broad days came before Friday's report. Against the flight-to-safety reading: nothing here shows who sold or where the money went. Against the analyst's lean: the dial's gathering near recent lows leaves room for a rebound, and the holiday record leans up.

2 · The dial

A dial with one quarter empty

The clearest picture of the week is one the instrument draws as a clock face. It ignores how far each stock moved and asks only where the stock is in its own recent swing.

Each dot on the dial is one stock. Its place around the face says where the price sits against its own average of the last twenty sessions. At the top it has just made a recent high. Down the right side it is falling away from that high. At the bottom it is at a recent low, and up the left side it is rising again. Stocks travel clockwise. The dial measures timing only: a stock that fell one percent and a stock that fell ten sit in the same place if they are at the same point of their swing.

An arrow, or hand, points to where a set of dots is gathered. A long hand means the set is bunched together; a short one means it is spread around the face. The figure has two views. In the first, two groups are colored and each has a hand: the loose side and the crowd side, the two ends of the map in chapter 3, where they are introduced properly. For now: the loose side is 61 hard-hit names led by Nvidia, Alphabet, Meta and Exxon, and the crowd side is 159 names that had been holding up, led by Apple, JPMorgan and Procter & Gamble. In the second view every stock is colored by its sector and the whole market gets two hands. The count hand gives every stock one vote. The cap hand weights each stock by the size of the company, so it shows where the money is gathered, not the names.

Play it from the start. Two Fridays ago the two sides sat on opposite faces of the dial: most of the crowd side near the top, just past recent highs, and most of the loose side near the bottom. The rebound of November 9 barely moves anything, because one good day does not change where a price sits against three weeks of its own history. From November 12 the crowd side begins to slide off the top. Through this week it strings out down the right-hand side while the loose side, which never left the bottom, tightens. On Friday 59 of the 61 loose-side names are in a single quarter.

Switch to the whole market and watch the two hands. All week the cap hand walked ahead and the count hand followed: on Monday the cap hand was already a third of the way round while the count hand was a quarter of the way, and by Friday the count hand had nearly caught up, both of them pointing at the bottom. The analyst's description, after stepping through the week one session at a time, was of the largest companies leading the rest down to the low like a shepherd. On Friday 60% of the market's value sat in the quarter just past a low, and less than 1% of it in the quarter that is rising.

Three things about Friday's dial have no earlier match in the six months it covers.

The rising quarter is empty. Eight stocks. On each of the week's five sessions it held between 8 and 17. Before this week its smallest count was 24, on September 9.

Both hands are long, and both point at the low. There have been bottom-heavy dials before; early October had more names past a low than Friday did. Friday is the only session where the count hand and the cap hand are each strongly bunched and each pointing within a tenth of a turn of the bottom. Names and money are in the same place.

The whole face turned at once. A typical stock moves about three hundredths of a turn in a session. On Friday the typical stock moved nine hundredths, the largest step of the 125 the dial records. Every group measured sped up: the loose side to three times its recent pace, the crowd side to a little more than twice.

Two quarters of the dial since late May

share of the 500 stocks in the rising quarter (teal) and in the quarter just past a low (ink), by session · today's drawing of each date · shaded = this week

That last point bears on a question the analyst raised from the board. The crowd side has been arriving at the low behind the loose side. One reading is that it is simply passing through in its turn, the way the two sides have alternated all year, and the loose side will be rising by the time it gets there. The other is that its descent was hurried, pulled or pushed, in which case the old rhythm is broken and a new one has to settle. The measurements are compatible with pressure that reached everyone, and they do not settle it. The crowd side moved faster than usual on four of the week's five sessions, not only on Friday. The gap between the two sides' hands has halved, from 0.46 of a turn on November 11 to 0.24 on Friday. And in price the two sides moved the same way two weeks running: up 4.5% and 1.6% in the rebound week, down 10.1% and 3.0% in this one. The direction is the same and the size differs by about three to one both times. That is the pattern a common pressure acting on two groups of different sensitivity would produce. It is an interpretation: nothing on the board identifies such a pressure or where it came from.

Two limits belong with all of this. The dial is built from price against its own recent average, so a hard decline carries a stock toward the bottom of the face by construction; the dial and the price table are one push seen in two ways, not two independent witnesses. And the newest readings move. Thursday's first reading placed 206 stocks just past a low; with Friday's prices added, Thursday now shows 99. A stock just past a low is at a recent low. Nothing on the dial says it is at the low.

3 · The map

Farther apart on the map, closer on the dial

The second picture does not use returns or timing at all, which is what makes it a useful check on the first. It asks how much of each stock's movement is the market's shared movement, and whether that stock's share of it rises and falls in step with everyone else's.

The motion map places each stock by two things. Vertically, its pressure: how caught up it is in what the whole market is doing, against that stock's own normal. The white line is the floor; below it a stock is under more shared pressure than usual, above it the stock is moving on its own. Horizontally, its coupling: how closely that stock's pressure follows the marketwide pressure over the last six months. Far right is the crowd, stocks breathing in time with the market. Far left are stocks keeping their own time. Being low or left on this map says nothing about whether a stock's price rose or fell.

For several weeks the analyst has read this map as having two gathering places, with stocks breaking toward one or the other: the crowd at the right, and a looser gathering out on the left, above the floor. This edition gives the two ends names so they can be followed from one picture to the next. The crowd side is every stock that stood right of +0.5 and below the floor on Friday: 159 names. The loose side is every stock left of −0.3 and above the floor: 61 names. Those are positions, and the instrument does not know what any company makes. But for this episode the positions can be labeled with what sits in them. The loose side is the hard-hit side: 23 technology companies, 13 industrials and 6 energy companies among its 61; 35 of them belong to the AI group; its typical member is down 19.7% since the record. The crowd side is the sheltered side: utilities, industrials, consumer companies, banks and insurers, property trusts and health care; 136 of its 159 belong to the rally group; its typical member is still 9.6% above the record. The pairing of loose with hard-hit and crowd with sheltered describes this autumn. In another episode the same two ends of the map could hold different companies and tell a different story.

Watch where the teal comes from. On October 21 the crowd was thin, 80 stocks, and half the market sat in the middle of the map. By the end of October the crowd had thinned further, to 58. Then it filled: 125 a week ago, 159 on Friday, a third of the index. Those stocks did not come from the other side. They came out of the middle, which has shrunk from half the market to 38%. The loose side travelled the other way: its typical member moved from −0.18 to −0.41 on the horizontal axis while the crowd side's moved from +0.36 to +0.67. The analyst's word for this, watching the trails lengthen in one direction or the other, was sorting.

Because the film's colors are chosen by where stocks ended, it cannot by itself show that the market is separating. The check that does not depend on that choice uses the two groups fixed by name on October 21. On that day the typical member of each stood at nearly the same place on the horizontal axis; the gap between them was close to zero. A week ago it was 0.46. On Friday it was 0.63, the widest yet: the rally group's typical member at +0.44, the AI group's at −0.18. A week in which both groups fell did not bring them together on this map. It pushed them further apart.

Coupling to the market, by group, since May

the typical member's position on the map's horizontal axis, six-month lens · gold = the rally group · blue = the AI group · above zero is toward the crowd

So the two pictures disagree in an informative way. On the dial the two sides are closing on each other. On the map they are separating. Both are true because they measure different things about the same stocks. The map says the two sides still respond to the market's shared pressure differently: they are still two kinds of stock. The dial says their price swings, which used to be offset, now arrive at their lows within days of each other. Division without the offset is the condition this edition is describing.

One caution belongs with any reading of this map. Its lens is a rolling six-month window, so a stock's position can also shift because an old stretch of sessions has dropped out of the back of the window rather than because of anything new. This week's move was checked for that: with the window's start held in place, the rally group's shift toward the crowd is nearly unchanged, and about half of the AI group's smaller shift the other way is old sessions leaving. The same check matters more from here. A dense run of sessions from late May and early June is now at the window's edge, and the whole map will move for that reason over the next two weeks.

A third tool, which sorts stocks into rooms by who moves in rhythm with whom, shows the reshuffle arriving on Friday. On a typical day about 64 of every 100 pairs of stocks that share a room still share one the next day. On Thursday it was 80. On Friday it was 62. The room led by consumer-discretionary companies, 79 stocks, split nearly in half. A new technology-led room of 75 stocks formed out of three older ones; Microsoft, Visa, Intel and Palantir are its largest members. The room led by financial companies kept 86% of its members. There are eight rooms, one more than a week ago, and the count says little: the membership is what moved.

4 · The memory

The decline writes itself into the short memory

The last reading has a time dimension. Every morning the instrument asks how far back the market is remembering: over what lookback its bursts of shared movement are most tightly organized against the index's distance from its high. Last week's edition showed two new structures at the edge of that picture and offered a plain explanation that could be checked. The check came back.

The picture is called the surface. Up the side is the lookback, from about six months at the bottom to more than two years at the top. Across is timing: on the left half the shared movement follows the index's drawdown, on the right half it leads it. Each cell is colored by the relationship at that lookback and timing: red where the two move together, blue where they move against each other. Red and blue are signs of a relationship, not market up and market down. For most of this year the picture has been dominated by the large red structure on the left: the market organized around an old memory, with the bursts trailing the drawdown by seven or eight months.

Last week's edition said both arrivals might simply be the pullback since October 6 entering the short lookbacks, and that if so they should fade if the index retook its high and keep growing if the pullback extended. The pullback extended by 8.6% and they grew. The blue structure in zone B went from a third of its zone to just over half, and the relationship inside it strengthened from −0.30 to −0.44. The red in zone A went from 46% to 58%. The established structure on the left did not give ground; on Tuesday it was the largest it has been in the past year.

Three zones at the edge and the structure in charge, August to Friday

share of cells showing a strong relationship in four fixed zones of the surface · ink = the established red structure on the left · red = zone A · blue = zone B · amber = zone C, at zero timing

The new feature is zone C. Two weeks ago it held no strong cell. A week ago it held 5%. On Friday it held about half, and it added to its count on every session of the week. This one sits at zero timing: over the last six months, the bursts of shared movement and the depth of the drawdown have been rising together, at the same moment. The analyst flagged it on the board as a red strengthening at the center, and also flagged two smaller changes: a faint new blue on the following side at the very shortest lookbacks, three sessions old, and the red patch that used to sit above zone B breaking up. That patch has gone from 15% of its area to 6% in a week.

The instrument's contest table also registered something on Friday that it had not listed before: a strong negative relationship at a lookback of 132 sessions, with the shared movement leading the drawdown by 75. It is a real feature and it is easy to over-read. Taken apart, four-fifths of its strength comes from just four pairs of days: the index's four deepest closes of this week, set against a stretch in early August when the market's shared movement was at its quietest of the summer. Each session this week added to it. That is the general lesson of this chapter. The structures at the edge are built largely from the decline itself, written into the instrument's shorter memories at different timings. Their growth is not separate evidence that the index will fall further, and they do not simply track it either: old sessions leaving the window and changes in the shared movement alter them too, and zone A's coverage eased on Friday while prices were still falling.

What would be evidence of a change is a matter of form. The analyst has watched reconstructed films of this surface covering more than five years. In those, a decline's recovery phase showed a new red structure arriving beneath a blue one that was fading. Zone C could be the first half of that. The second half has not started: the blue beside it is still deepening. In the earlier cases the sequence took weeks.

The lookback the instrument settles on as the market's working memory is unchanged at about eleven months, and its hold strengthened.

The second book: a field of agreement

The instrument keeps a second book that ignores timing altogether. It asks how much the five hundred stocks disagree about the size of their own swings, at sixteen lookbacks from one month to three years. Disagreement is the normal state. Days when it drops below its own trailing floor are logged as agreement days, and in the instrument's own census those days have sat at the onsets of the market's stormier stretches. Agreement marks structure. It does not say which way.

Drawn as a field, with agreement in rust and loud disagreement in blue, the newest edge of this book usually arrives blue. The analyst noticed that this week it arrived rust, and not only at the edge. Counted, that holds: on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday all sixteen lookbacks sat on the agreement side of their own histories, and on Tuesday and Wednesday seven of them were deep on that side. Agreement days were logged on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, a cluster of the kind the board has shown before.

Two cautions keep it in proportion. The field is drawn smoothed over five sessions; Friday's own unsmoothed reading reopened disagreement at the shortest lookbacks, so the agreement belt and Friday's reopening are both on the board at once. And the agreement days are reconstructions. On each of those mornings the book's first reading was still apart; Monday's agreement first appeared in the reading of Thursday's close and the other two only in the reading of Friday's, once later prices had been added. The cluster is a feature of today's drawing of the week, and a reader following the board each morning did not see it arrive.

A related count changed sharply. A week ago 42 stocks had swings unusually quiet against their own history and 19 unusually loud. On Friday it was 11 and 11. That looks balanced. Against their own records the two counts are not alike: eleven is high for the loud end and low for the quiet end. The quiet stocks are what disappeared.

5 · What would change this read

Last week's four markers, and next week's four

Last week's edition ended with four things to watch and three ways the market could go. Here is what each marker did, which branch the week fit, and what to watch now.

what was watcheda week agowhat happened
The two blocs, by name: the 68 home-and-consumer stocks and the 58 hardware stocks that each moved as a unit+13% and −16% since the recordBoth fell. The home-and-consumer list lost 3.1% and the hardware list 12.4%, with no member of the hardware list higher on the week. The lists held their names: 59 of 68 and 56 of 58 are still on them.
Wednesday's session, after Nvidia's resultsthe hardware list fell 9.4% on Nov 5 and rose 6.2% on Nov 9Nothing happened on Wednesday: both lists moved less than a third of one percent. The move as a unit came on Friday, when the hardware list's typical member lost 6.9%.
The leaders against interest ratesthe two-year yield 4.88%Yields fell to 4.63% and the leaders fell anyway, alongside the hardware names on Tuesday and Thursday. That was the difference between last week's first and second branches.
The edge of the surfacetwo new structures filling 32% and 46% of their zonesBoth kept their strength and form and grew, to 52% and 58%, and a third arrived at zero timing. The established structure reached its largest of the past year.

Against last week's three branches, the week left the first, still two, and moved toward the second, one market, without arriving there. The second branch asked for down days to become shared. Two of this week's were, more completely than any in six months. It also asked for the biggest shared pattern to swell and begin absorbing the hardware names, and for the two crowds to converge. Neither happened: that pattern's share is no larger, the second pattern is stronger, and the map's two sides are further apart. The week was something the three branches did not name: two groups, with more of their movement shared.

Branch 1Back in turn

The loose side leaves its low first. The rising quarter fills with its names, they hold on the next readings and their prices rise as they do, while the crowd side finishes its own descent behind them. The offset between the two sides returns, and with it the cushion.

Branch 2Down together

The loose side stays at its low while the crowd side arrives beside it. The rising quarter stays empty, the one-directional days keep coming, and the typical stock gives up what remains of its gain since the record. This is what the analyst's lean expects.

Branch 3A new order

The two sides trade places in their timing, or settle into an arrangement that is not the old alternation, and keep it across several readings. One crossing, or one redrawn morning, would not establish it.
  1. The empty quarter.now: 8 of 500 stocks rising in their own swing · never below 24 before this week · 265 just past a low

    Who enters first, do they stay on the next readings, and do prices rise as they enter? In the one earlier case in the dial's record, early October, it took seven to thirteen sessions to go from a bottom-heavy dial to a fifth of all names rising. The loose side is the closest to the line.

  2. The first up day: the index against the typical stock.now: loose side 59 of 61 just past a low · crowd side 116 of 159 still at a high or falling

    The loose side is nearest the rising quarter and holds several of the largest companies. The crowd side has not reached a low. If prices turn, the index could rise while most stocks are still falling. Count how many rise, and compare the typical stock with the index.

  3. The order of the two sides.now: their hands 0.24 of a turn apart on the dial, from 0.46 on Nov 11 · 0.63 apart on the map, the widest yet

    Does the loose side move off the bottom as the crowd side reaches it, or do they sit there together? That separates branch 1 from branch 2.

  4. The edge of the surface.now: zone B 52% and still deepening · zone C about half full, from 5% a week ago · the second book's agreement belt · no crest-clustering event logged for seven sessions

    Repair would show as the blue in zone B beginning to fade while the red in zone C holds. Continued growth in all three zones says only that the decline is still in the window. Does the agreement belt in the second book persist, or does Friday's reopening spread? A newly logged event, and which stocks supply it, would be new information either way.

Observed

  • The week by group and by day; the index and its typical stock.
  • The common share of each session over six months, and the story count.
  • The dial, session by session: quarter counts, both hands, the step of the typical stock, the two sides' hands.
  • The map by side and by the October 21 groups, with the window-exit check; the rooms.
  • The surface in four fixed zones since August, and the dated pairs behind its newest feature.
  • The second book's field of agreement by lookback, and its logged agreement days.

Interpretation

  • The two groups are still two, and the offset between them weakened.
  • The week's movement is compatible with a common pressure reaching two groups of different sensitivity. The board does not identify one.
  • The dial's gathering near recent lows is a condition. It leaves room for a rebound and does not establish that the decline is over.
  • The surface's edge structures are the decline restated, not a separate signal.
  • The labels hard-hit and sheltered, and the readings of Nvidia and of the move to safety, are the analyst's, not measurements.

Not established

  • A direction, a mechanism, a forecast, or the date of a low.
  • That the crowd side's descent was pushed rather than due; the measurements lean that way and do not settle it.
  • That Friday's dial will look the same once later sessions are added; Thursday's did not.
  • That zone C is the start of a recovery pattern, or that the second book's agreement will last.
  • That any outside event caused the week, or what supplied the shared movement; the broad days came before Friday's news.
  • Who sold, or where the money went.

The instrument's words

A short glossary

The rally group · the AI group
The two groups the instrument fixed by name on October 21: 314 stocks that had carried October's advance and 114 that had fallen, including Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, Meta and Alphabet. Held fixed since, so nothing is re-sorted after the fact.
The loose side · the crowd side
The two ends of the map as it stood on November 20: 61 stocks left of −0.3 and above the floor, and 159 stocks right of +0.5 and below it. In this episode they are the hard-hit names and the sheltered names. They are positions chosen on one day and followed backward, and the pairing with those descriptions belongs to this episode only.
The typical stock
The median: the stock in the middle when the five hundred are lined up by return.
Common share
How much of one session's movement, with each stock measured in units of its own usual daily swing, is a single shift shared by all stocks. Near zero when stocks go their own ways; near one when they all make the same move.
Story count · first and second pattern
The effective number of independent patterns in the stocks' daily returns: the fast reader uses 21 sessions, the slow reader 63. The first pattern is the biggest shared movement; the second is the biggest left once the first is removed. Each morning's reading uses returns through the session before.
The dial · a quarter · a hand
Each stock placed by where its price sits against its own twenty-session average: just past a high, falling, just past a low, rising. Timing only; size is ignored. A hand points to where a set of stocks is gathered and its length is how tightly. The count hand gives each stock one vote; the cap hand weights by company size.
The map · pressure · the floor · coupling · the crowd
Each stock's participation in the market's shared moves against its own normal (vertical), and how closely its pressure follows the marketwide pressure over a rolling six-month window (horizontal). Below the floor is above-normal pressure. The crowd is the right-hand edge, coupling above +0.5.
Rooms
Groups of stocks that move in rhythm with one another, re-sorted each session and matched to the previous session's groups. A room is labeled by its largest sector.
The surface · lookback · lead and lag
The relationship between the market's bursts of shared movement and the index's drawdown from its high, at every lookback and every timing at once. Red is a positive relationship, blue a negative one. Lag means the bursts follow the drawdown; lead, that they run ahead of it.
The second book · agreement days
A separate measure of how much the stocks disagree about the size of their own swings, at sixteen lookbacks. An agreement day is one on which that disagreement falls below its own trailing floor. Drawn as a field, agreement is rust and loud disagreement blue.
A crest-clustering event
The one kind of event the instrument logs: a session on which an unusually large number of stocks sit at the top of their own swing together. The map's vertical readings drift upward on days without one.
A print · a redraw
The morning's first reading of the newest day is its print. Several measures are recomputed as later sessions arrive, so the newest day is always the least settled thing on the board. Where a figure here is a print, the text says so.

Reading notes, sources and construction

  • The instrument reads daily closing prices for a pool of about 650 names: the current S&P 500 and former members for which prices are available. 500 current names are shown on the dial and the map. Every number here is regenerated from the raw price files on prices 252a44ec, Saturday's build of the November 20 close. One stock's Friday price is missing from the vendor feed and was carried forward unchanged: Sandisk, on the first day of trading after its share split. Its Friday readings are stale and it is not named in any list here; no median in this edition moves on one stock.
  • Chapter 1. The week's returns: index −1.92%, −1.03%, −0.23%, −2.02%, −3.70%; shares of the 500 higher 30%, 15%, 47%, 7%, 25%. Friday's decline is the 53rd largest of 6,762 sessions since 2000 on this series and the largest since November 5; the five-session decline is the largest since the five ending April 8, 2025; seven straight lower closes is the longest run since February 2020. The common share is the squared mean of the standardized returns of the 500 over the mean of their squares, each stock standardized by its own trailing 63-session standard deviation: 0.18, 0.51, 0.01, 0.60, 0.37 for the week against a 126-session median of 0.07; the six highest are Nov 19, Nov 17, Nov 9, Jun 17, Nov 5, Nov 20. The correlation between the two groups' daily median returns, in 21-session blocks ending Jun 24, Jul 24, Aug 24, Sep 23, Oct 22 and Nov 20: +0.08, −0.50, +0.04, +0.28, −0.14, +0.53; the medians had the same sign on 43 to 71% of days in every block. The story count uses returns through Thursday, the instrument's convention (5.81 and 11.01); with Friday included it reads 5.89 and 10.77, with the first two patterns at 33.6% and 20.5% of the 21-session variation. The 63-session count was last lower on August 6, 2025.
  • Chapter 2. A stock's place on the dial is the phase of its price against a 20-session average; the four quarters are equal quarter-turns from the high. All dial figures are today's drawing of each date, counted at full precision from the same phases the moving figure plays: Friday 89, 138, 265 and 8 names by quarter, the same as that morning's first print. Rising-quarter counts for Nov 16–20: 13, 12, 17, 8, 8; the smallest before that, 24 on Sep 9. Hands on Friday: count 0.55 at 0.48 of a turn, cap 0.66 at 0.51; through the week the count hand stood at 0.24, 0.30, 0.31, 0.36, 0.48 of a turn and the cap hand at 0.32, 0.35, 0.37, 0.38, 0.51. Friday is the only one of 126 sessions with both hands at 0.5 or longer and both between 0.40 and 0.60 of a turn. Median step of the 500 on Friday 0.09 of a turn against a 125-step median of 0.03; by set, Friday against each set's median over the prior twenty sessions: loose side 3.0 times, crowd side 2.3, AI group 3.4, rally group 3.3. The two sides' hands: loose 0.94 long at 0.60, crowd 0.55 at 0.36; gap 0.46 on Nov 11, 0.32 on Nov 13, 0.24 on Nov 20. The October 21 groups on Friday's dial: AI group 9, 17, 86 and 2 by quarter; rally group 75, 107, 130 and 2.
  • Chapter 3. Coupling is the correlation of a stock's pressure with the marketwide measure over 126 sessions. The loose side holds 22.5% of the 500's market value and the crowd side 19.2%; 21 of the loose side's 61 belong to the rally group and 8 of the crowd side's 159 to the AI group. Week returns by side: −10.1% and −3.0% (medians); the week before, +4.5% and +1.6%. Shares of the 500 left of zero, in the middle and in the crowd: 36, 48 and 16% on Oct 21; 30, 38 and 32% on Nov 20. Gap between the October 21 groups' medians: −0.07, 0.46, 0.63 on Oct 21, Nov 13 and Nov 20. Window-exit check, Nov 13 to 20: rally group +0.065 on the rolling window and +0.062 with the window's start held; AI group −0.020 and −0.011. A year-long version of the same lens also drifted right this week; that drift came entirely from sessions leaving its window and is not reported as a finding. The crest-clustering events are the instrument's closure days. On Saturday's build November 13 is no longer one of them (49 qualifying stocks against a threshold of 51; the two builds before it had 56 and 59), so the last event is November 11; earlier builds dated it to November 13. Every map position since then is drawn from the newer classification.
  • Chapter 4. Zone A is lookbacks 168 to 216 at leads of 122 to 147 sessions (46.2% of cells strongly positive on Nov 13, 57.7% on Nov 20); zone B is lookbacks 120 to 180 at leads of 47 to 93 (31.7% and 52.2% strongly negative; mean −0.30 and −0.44); zone C is lookbacks 120 to 144 at timings of −14 to +10 (0, 5.3 and 53.3% on Nov 6, 13 and 20); the established structure is lookbacks 120 to 600 at lags of 72 to 180 (23.8% and 24.6%; year high 25.5% on Nov 17). A strong relationship is a correlation of 0.45 or beyond, counted over cells with enough data. The series mixes reconstructed frames with each recent morning's retained reading, so price vintages differ. The 132-session feature reads −0.83 at a lead of 75; of that, −0.66 comes from the pairs joining the drawdown of Nov 17–20 to the shared-movement readings of Aug 3–6; with the window ended on Nov 13 the same cell reads −0.47. The working memory is 228 sessions at +0.913 against 420 sessions at +0.889. Quiet and loud are stocks whose swing size is more than two standard deviations below or above their own history, on a pool of 637; against the board's own record eleven loud names is near the 84th percentile and eleven quiet near the 12th. The second book's field is the percentile of each lookback's disagreement against its own history, displayed as a centered five-session median; "the agreement side" is below the 50th percentile and "deep" below the 20th, descriptive cuts chosen for this table and not the instrument's own threshold; counts by the second read on today's reconstruction. Friday's unsmoothed reading averages the 75th percentile across lookbacks, with the 31- and 42-session lookbacks near the 99th. Agreement days in today's reconstruction: Nov 16, 17 and 19. The book's first print read apart on every morning of the week (spread 1.63, 1.50, 1.38, 1.17 and 1.26 against a floor near 1.09); Thursday's now reads 0.90. The storm-onset census is the board's own: all 13 measurable onsets had an agreement day within ten sessions.

The two groups are comms/sol_20261025/map_dial_named_endpoints.csv. How this edition was made. Jason Connerty built the instrument, ran its chain on the Friday close, and walked the board; the two gathering places on the map, the cap hand leading the count hand, the question of whether the crowd side was passing through or being pushed, the rust across the second book and the readings of the surface are his. An independent second read made its own pass before his, then checked each of his observations against the record. Claude (Fable 5.2) ran the numbers, built the moving figures and wrote the edition.

A Burst Monitor read · written Sunday, November 22, 2026 from the Friday, November 20 close · a position read on history, never a forecast, not investment advice · the newest day's readings restate as later sessions are added; where a figure is a first print, the text says so.
